objectives: Segment spoken short /o/ CVC words into phonemes.
Map each phoneme to its grapheme and spell the word.
Distinguish short /o/ from short /a/ during encoding.
Use read-back to detect and repair spelling errors.
concepts: Encoding moves from spoken phonemes to written graphemes.
The middle vowel must be represented accurately.
Minimal contrasts reveal vowel encoding errors.

definitions.definition: Representing spoken phonemes with written graphemes.
Separating a spoken word into its individual sounds.
Reading a written word to verify that it represents the intended sounds.

workedExamples: hat for hot → compare the middle sound and replace a with o.
commonMistakes: Confusing o with another short vowel.
Writing before segmenting the spoken word.
revisionPoints: Spoken word → phonemes → graphemes → spelling → read-back.

basic: Spell hot, mop, pot and dog from dictation.
conceptual: Identify the vowel causing an encoding error.
application: Encode taught short /o/ CVC words independently.
higherOrderThinking: Choose the correction step for an o/a spelling error.
mixedReview: Spell short /o/ and contrast with short /a/ words.

mistakeBasedRevision: hot → hat error: check the middle vowel.
mop → map error: check the middle vowel.
weakTopicRevision: Repeat auditory contrast before spelling the target word again.

activities.name: Sound-box encoding
steps: Push one counter for each phoneme.

outcomes: Learner segments short /o/ CVC words with at least 80% accuracy.
Learner spells taught short /o/ CVC words with at least 80% accuracy.
Learner represents short /o/ with o in the middle position.
Learner uses read-back to identify and correct an encoding error.

questions.question: Which word uses o for its middle sound?
What should you do first when spelling a spoken CVC word?
options: Say it and segment its sounds

questions.question: After segmenting /m/ /o/ /p/, what should you do?
options: Map each sound to a grapheme and write it

questions.question: A learner writes “hat” for “hot.” Which sound needs checking?
A learner writes “map” for “mop.” What should be checked?
Which spelling has short /o/ in the middle?
Why should the learner read the written word back?
options: To check that the spelling represents the intended sounds

questions.question: Which pair is useful for checking short /o/ spelling against short /a/?
Which spelling begins d, has short /o/, and ends g?
What should happen if the written word does not sound like the target word?
options: Re-segment, check the graphemes and rewrite it

questions.question: What is the main goal of this lesson?
options: Encode taught short /o/ CVC words accurately using sound-to-letter mapping
